title: Review: TP-LINK TG-3468 10/100/1000Mbps Gigabit PCI Express Network Adapter
text:
I'm going to have to say this is the best value in this product space. The Realtek chip used is really quite reliable, and I'm not easy to please. The Intel chip is better performance wise, but only by about 5% on the top end, however costs at least double, if not more. 95% of people won't be able to tell the difference in the performance even if they try pretty hard, and in the application this will be used, it won't be an issue anyway since maximum network traffic bursts will be in the 20MB/s range, at least for a few years. It's power consumption, about 1 watt at idle or very low traffic, is quite acceptable, and I'm also a stickler about that. An exceedingly simple card like this is hard to screw up, and they didn't, so that's a good sign. If you really need those 5,000 additional management features available on the Intel based card, go ahead and spend 4x what this one costs. Or is it 5x? I think I paid $10 for this one. Once, only once, did we try a card based on the Via chip. That card is in the trash now.

Pay no attention to people saying it didn't work on their Windows box. If someone doesn't have the expertise to get the driver on to their Windows box, they shouldn't be adding cards to their box by themselves as it is. Any up-to-date version of Windows 7 or later has the driver already. And, of course, the card comes with a mini-cd with the driver on it, and it can be downloaded off the internet quite easily. If you're trying to add this card to a box that is 10 years old, well, bravo to you, but you will have to get creative unless you are running software that's newer than your box. We use Linux, and the driver has been in Linux distros for at least a year now. Even if the Linux release that you're running is a couple of years old, if you've been updating your kernel like you should be, you have the driver.

The drive has a plastic body, even the USB A plug, the big one, is plastic on the outside. Not unsafe, but doesn't help with cooling. I have another drive by another manufacturer. It has an aluminum case, so keeps cooler.

To make it work, copy whatever data you want do it, but point a fan at it until it's done.

Sandisk, if you're reading this, I'd rather throttle transfer speeds than worry what and how much data was successfully copied. Just an idea.

text:
I was looking forward to this product because of the features of 360 degree view, being able to communicate through the app both ways, and it being able to plug into a light socket. I didn’t know exactly which socket I would spare but was willing to make the sacrifice of a prime light area if the camera worked well enough. Surprisingly, the camera came with an attachment that allowed this to be plugged into a wall rather than a light fixture! I loved that about it but came to realize it was not strong enough to support the weight of the camera, especially if it was moving at all, so it started to slowly fall out of the socket. That was strike one for me.
Strike two was trying to set up the camera (which, to be fair, was a pretty easy setup even though I think it asked for a bit too much information for this type of product), if I used the app to change the camera’s view, it would rotate the camera and would ultimately rotate the image on my screen to an off-kilter image. I guess I expected it to do automatic re-calibration and that is quite a bit to expect so it’s not necessarily the product’s fault for this issue.
Yet my third strike was the thing I was most excited for—360 degree views—not being possible (or at least not as far as I could figure out). One would think the app would be pretty straightforward where you press the up, down, left, and right buttons to direct your camera to those directions but they only went so far. I would say some of the angles I tried would not even go 180 degrees which was disheartening. title: One of my go-to cameras - not any more - updated
text:
3/01/2023 update
Updated to firmware 17.0, battery seems to be slightly better.
However, all cameras will go offline all the time. Glad I still have LaView cameras to cover some important area. I changed the rating from 2 stars to 1 star, because we don’t have negative stars rating option.

9/30/2022 update

Changed from 5 star to 2 star.
1 for best sound communication
1 for final refund

It took me 5 emails to have someone reply.
Then they disappeared.
Found the Dzees person and directly asked about the issue, no answer received. Only offered refund.

Issue:
From certain point, the battery drained like crazy (maybe after some firmware update). They drained 10% each day, for 2 of my cameras. So I know it’s something unusual, not accidents.

They used to last for 3-4 weeks, for light use. So I know they don’t have a good battery life, but for the best sound communication, I was fine. But 10% battery for each day with NO USE at all, that’s not acceptable.

I thought it was the security issue, that someone might hacked into my Dzees cameras, because my other brands cameras are still fine, but even after putting it into “sleep mode”, it still drained the battery similarly.

I have to give up. Unless they have improved the flaw and prove its security, I will stay away from now on.

—- original review—-
There are several things need to be mentioned about this camera and brand.

1. Their app is not a universal version that lots brands use. The design is very intuitive and easy to check event recording videos, which is a huge plus when your app requires you to drag the time line to align the event and won’t allow you to fast forward the playback.

2. The camera mount base is one of the best in design. The materials used is still plastic, not sure if it’s for weight reduction, but it works okay. The holes sizes are matching screws unlike many others. The connector adjustment and camera rotational installation both can be adjusted, which makes it a lot easier. I have used one of their magnetic base which has bright and down sides. For security purpose, the screw-in installation is still my favorite.

3. Motion trigger is average. Will pick up the videos when packages are delivered, but mostly starts when delivery person is turning after dropping the packages. It’s mostly the motion detection range that caused this. Improvement on the detection algorithm should solve this fairly easy, if they want to make the improvement.

4. The only brand that offers 7 days cloud storage for free. Most (almost) other brands require subscription to access cloud storage, or you have to insert a SD card in the camera or base station (like Eufy, LaView, etc) to not worry about losing the video footage when cameras were taken or damaged. This might be a huge plus for a lot of people who want to save the sub fee which accumulates quickly.

5. This could be a mixed one, but with subscription, you will have the AI motion detection. I tried it for 30 days and I really like it, it tells you if it’s human, or pets, or vehicles. The notifications also pop on your Apple Watch if you use iphone and wear an Apple Watch. But I want some better motion detection range cameras so I didn’t subscribe to this service. I don’t subscribe normally, but for this AI detection I might choose to sub.

6. One of the best customer service I have met. YMMV always but it’s my experience.

Some that I am not a fan:

1. As mentioned earlier, the motion detection range/speed is average. Some other brands I used will start recording when delivery person start to bend over and drop the packages.

2. You click “play” icon to live stream the camera. You need to click the “stop” block icon to stop the stream. This is not a huge deal, but most apps just return to last page and live stream will stop automatically.

3. Battery is not 6 months for sure. Frequent motion detection trains the battery 20% in 2 weeks. Although this could just be my situation, I used some other brands and after 4 weeks of similar motion triggering, only 10% battery was drained. However, it’s unfair to make a final conclusion because how battery use programmed are different among all brands, some will stay on 100% for a bit longer so it has to be fully drained to know if the battery life is really long or short. So my experience is only for reference purpose.

Considering major big brands cameras are generally 50%-100% more expensive, I would say if you don’t want to spend too much, or you just want to try the battery cameras see if they work for you, Dzees would be one of my options. Hope my 2 cents help.

title: Trouble with setup, once it’s up it works fine
text:
Firstly the packaging looks great, actually looks very legitimate product unlike typical Bluetooth adapters that seems to be just thrown together in cheap packaging.

I was hoping it would be a simple plug and play, but I was unfortunately disappointed. It wouldn’t get picked up correctly by Windows 10 with all of its latest updates.

Since I use Bluetooth keyboard and speaker with my previous Bluetooth adapter, when this adapter didn’t work out the gate, it caused all sorts of problems. Because I couldn’t use my keyboard, I had a lot of trouble trying to troubleshoot. Even plugging my old Bluetooth adapter, it wasn’t recognizing my previously paired connections.

Through the struggle, I managed to get my old adapter working, and searched for the drivers on Ugreen’s website. Coupled with the “appropriate” drivers, I tried the install again.

This time, I got another error message. Something about an unauthorized Bluetooth device has been installed, so the drivers couldn’t be installed. After searching online, and trying out the solutions: disabling and uninstalling any Bluetooth related devices, it finally worked.

Now it’s setup, it seems to work fine. I haven’t experienced disconnects, and my keyboard and speaker is working fine. No issues at all with audio, which is a problem I was having with my old adapter (at random times).

If you’re willing to possibly put in some work to get it working, it might be the newest 5.3 Bluetooth adapter you can get.

The screen clamp has a hole in it - the hole goes over/around your camera lens and the ring light angle can be adjusted by manually moving it.  The clamp maintains firm, but seemingly safe pressure on the laptop screen.  The power cable is approximatley 6' long and has a built in light control switch panel.  I think this is a good ring light, overall - it does a good job at what it is supposed to do.  Recommended!

title: Almost perfect
text:
I needed to support a good number of chargers for; phone, tablet, networking switch, back up drives, NAS, etc. I would say this is a great power strip. Only it had one little flaw - it became intermittent. Do to it's low cost, I decided to fix it rather than sending it back. It has 4 security screws and another 4 hidden under it's feet. I have the proper security bit so I opened it and found the hot lead coming in from the power cord going to the switch had a cold solder joint and wasn't always making contact.

[A cold solder joint is when not enough heat was applied during the soldering. The finish is dull instead of shiny and the joint could possibly break, especially under stress.] All other joints looked fine. I soldered the one joint back together and reassembled the power strip. It works well now. I consider this issue a one off and feel in general that the quality is good. So after this happened I purchased a second one. I realize that I probably voided the warrantee and I'm ok with that.

Note for the manufacturer: better quality control would have quickly spotted this.

title: Wifi 6e is not backwards compatible with Wifi6
text: The boxes (outer printed one and inner white one) were unbelievably complicated to open..no taped sides, e.g., and I had to tear them finally. The setup was fiddly (and I am an IT network manager). I turned off Smart Connection as it causes so many problems with legacy devices. None of my devices could see the 5gHz network..googled and found I had to switch to 40 and not Auto for the band, then the network name showed up. I did choose WPA2/WPA3 compatible (the simplest base choice offered) but our home alarm system from QOLSYS, bathrooms scales and a few others never could see even the 2.4gHz network despite all using the previous unit's WPA2 security--tried rebooting them, this unit, nothing worked. When I switched this unit off, they all immediately saw the other base unit and connected. The setup routine alerted me that this unit as shipped had hardware v 1.0, but the current hardware was at 1.6. No chance of upgrading the hardware, obviously or getting some bugs fixed that way. Then, I thought all the protocols were backwards compatible but with prompt email support from TPLink over a weekend (and despite conflicting info from Apple) I was told my brand new iPad Air 5 which does Wifi6, indeed would not see the Wifi6e network from this device. Nor did my still-new iMac which does Wifi6, would not see Wifi6e. Apples and oranges for Wifi6e vs Wifi6. With the older legacy devices not even working with its2.4 network, let alone a brand new iPad Air 5 unable to use WiFi6e, I returned this unit.

title: Best Small 1080p TV
text:
Usually 720p is sufficient resolution for a small TV, which is often a secondary set used in a kitchen or such, rather than for primary, critical viewing. There is a 720p version of this model that is usually a few dollars cheaper.

But you may need 1080p. If you want the TV to double as a computer monitor, for example. Or if you're feeding it a signal shared with other 1080p displays (because HDMI sources will select the lowest common resolution of all connected displays).

So if you need a 32" 1080p TV, this is the least expensive choice commonly available. Fortunately, it forces few compromises. The picture quality is decent. The internal audio is surprisingly adequate for non-music programming. The brightness is sufficient for a fully lit room, such as a kitchen. It can accept any common signal source via HDMI or RF. It has a headphone jack and a serviceable remote control.

Its only shortfall is its rudimentary calibration controls, so you'll have to accept one of the picture pre-sets, with just a few adjustments available. Fortunately, the presets include a range of options, one of which should suit most situations. Again, it's not a unit intended for critical viewing.

I've used Roku streaming devices before, but this was my first experience with the Roku operating system. I'm fairly impressed with its ability to set up and control the TV in a number of useful ways: timers, default input, power-saving, etc. And of course the Roku streaming platform is arguably the best in the world. It was no problem to activate my old Roku account (unused for several years), set up the TV, and then add my current accounts for services like Netflix, Amazon, Disney+, HBOMax, and Hulu. (Yes, I spend too much on streaming services. So shoot me: it's a pandemic out there!) There are of course dozens of services available via Roku, many of them free.

And it's very handy to have YouTube on the kitchen TV.

My old eyes wanted a bigger screen to replace our 10-year old 22-inch Vizio that was our kitchen TV for the last decade. This was the biggest that would fit in the cubby. It had to be 1080p to take the split feed from our TiVo in the living room. This TV, for these and all the reasons outlined above, exceeded all my expectations and met all my needs at a very reasonable price.

title: Exceeds my expectations
text:
This has to be the first time I've ever received a Windows PC in my mailbox from the postman. That's how I received the Kamrui Mini PC. I ordered this PC to connect to a monitor I had in a guest room for company to have access to their email and the internet during their stays. It suits my purpose very well and I am extremely pleased with it. It looks like a toy but don't let looks fool you. It performs well beyond my expectations..

This Kamrui Mini PC is approximately 5" wide, slightly larger than my Roku Ultra streaming box. It comes with a power block and lengthy cable as well as a small mounting plate and screws to connect it to the back of a monitor. The unit has an 11th generation Intel Celeron N5105 processor, 8 GB DDR4 RAM and 256 GB SSD. It uses Intel integrated graphics, and has both Bluetooth and WiFi connectivity. My unit connected effortlessly to my network.

There is a power button and four USB ports (including two USB 3 and two USB 2 ports), two HDMI ports, an AV jack, LAN port, and DC power port. Underneath the PC is a compartment where you can install an additional 2.5" SSD. I was able to plug in a mouse, keyboard, computer speakers and an HDMI cable to my monitor without problems. There was plenty of room. The PC powers on and boots very quickly and was able to synch nicely with a 4K monitor. The PC is loaded with Windows 11 Pro and downloaded a handful of Windows 11 updates reasonably fast. It made quick work of downloading several apps I needed. It mercifully does not have much bloatware. There is a glowing blue light under the cover that illuminates when the device is powered on.

The manufacturer offers a two-year warranty. For someone who is looking for a modest PC for light duties such as checking emails and surfing the internet and who has a spare monitor available, this little unit is just what the doctor ordered. I recommend it highly and award it 5 stars.

title: Excellent noise blocking for snoring or other annoyances
text:
Okay so, for the first few months I struggled with these earbuds, but my problem was that I was listening to brown noise with a lower sound/frequency. I finally found some brown noise to listen to while I sleep, and it’s been amazing!

My partner snores very loudly to the point where before I was barely getting 8 hours of sleep and I would have to wake him every so often so he could lay on his side (still snoring of course but a little less annoying). I found these earbuds and decided to give them a try. I love them so much! I can finally sleep with my partner and guarantee we both will get our 8 hours of sleep.

They have these double blockers made around the earbud speaker itself which helps it to “plug” into your ear. This was an absolute win for me both for noise cancellation and comfort. Speaking of, these earbuds have a bendy soft rubber material around it , the ends being semi flexible so when you lay on your side you don’t feel any hard poking near your ear.

A tip: position these earbuds in your ear so that the ends are horizontal on your ear (ear hole to outer ear) when sleeping. It’s the most comfy imo.

Don’t forget to clean these every so often or you’ll get extremely itchy ears at night.

Overall these have solved my snoring issue, I wish this company would make a wireless version of these, as the cord does limit my movement at night and I tend to try to get comfy frequently in bed (turning on other side etc). The music/audio quality honestly isn’t bad at all, I’ve watched plenty of videos with these on and they’ve sounded as good if not better than my regular skull candy buds.

Give it a shot if you’re wanting peace and quiet, just make sure you have a loud enough ambiance sound playing in the background! I love these earbuds!!!

text:
The Ingnok 16-inch IPS Portable Monitor is an excellent choice for anyone who needs a portable and good quality monitor that works with a variety of devices. The monitor has a 1200P resolution and 16:10 aspect ratio, which provides crisp and clear images, making it ideal anyone who needs more real estate when working with portable devices.

One of the best features of the Ingnok 16-inch IPS Portable Monitor is its compatibility with a variety of devices. It comes with mini-HDMI and 2 Type-C ports, making it easy to connect to laptops, Android phones and other compatible devices. This versatility means that you can use the monitor for both work and play, whether you're playing games on your portable consoles, watching videos from your phone or working on your laptop.

Another advantage of the Ingnok 16-inch IPS Portable Monitor is its portability. The monitor is lightweight and slim, making it easy to carry with you wherever you go. Whether you're traveling for work or pleasure, the monitor is a convenient accessory to have on hand.

The monitor's IPS display technology ensures that you get clear and vivid images from most angles, making it suitable for sharing with others, which is especially useful if you are working on a project with colleagues or friends.

The OSD settings are very easy access and play with the settings. You might need to play a bit with the OSD settings, if you want to closely match its colors with another monitor.

The audio is clear but tiny, which it is expected from a slim portable monitor and when dial to 100% brightness it works very well even in well lit rooms.

Included with the monitor you will find a very useful mini-HDMI to HDMI cable, a USB-C to USB-C cable, a USB-A to USB-C cable and power adpater.

The Ingnok 16-inch IPS Portable Monitor could operate by drawing power from compatible USB-C devices. This allows the monitor to operate with a single cable for power and video.
In case you use the mini-HDMI to HDMI cable, you will have to use the included power adapter to power the monitor. It could also work with a portable power bank.

The Ingnok 16-inch IPS Portable Monitor is an excellent unit for anyone who needs a good quality portable display. Its compatibility with a variety of devices, high-resolution and portability makes it a versatile and convenient accessory for work or play.

title: Very useful tool to test if devices are delivering or getting appropriate power.
text:
If you are encountering issues with USB devices, cables or chargers, a USB voltage meter or tester could come handy to diagnose the problem.

The Plugable USB C Power Meter Tester is like a voltmeter in a USB thumb drive body. It has matte plastic shell with rounded corners and smooth edges.
It has a bright and clear screen that displays the measured voltage, amps and watts.
The shell is matte black plastic, with rounded corners and smooth edges.

The device is bi-directional so it can work on both directions and it has a button on the side to flip the screen.

There is a single USB-C tip and a single USB-C port on the other side, so it will only works with USB-C interface.

The Plugable USB C Power Meter Tester has a wide testing range, since it can go anywhere from 5 to 48 volts, at a current of 0 to 6.1 amps for a whooping 240W. This range makes very useful for testing new and future devices and also testing overvoltage.

This USB tester is very accurate and it supports a wider range of voltages and wattages.
It is very portable, easy to use with a clear and bright display.

title: Average quality images from a compact, lightweight, easily mounted dashcam
text: I was interested to see if this unit was as good or better than an inexpensive dashcam a couple of years ago.  Since the purpose of a dashcam is to record images in case of an accident, picture quality is important. Ideally, the images should be good enough to identify people and vehicles and read license plate numbers.  I ran several tests with this camera in my windshield and found that the images seem to be rather low quality.  If a car in traffic was right in front of me at a stop light and the ambient lighting was favorable, I could usually make out the license plate number.  In any case, the make and model of the car were identifiable.  That said, I tried to make out the license plate numbers for cars that had just passed mine and moved into my lane and could not do so. The first situation is important if I collided with a car that stopped abruptly right in front of me.  The second situation is important if another passing car clipped my car on the way by.  The point of having a dashcam is to record evidence of fault in case of an accident.  This camera has some useful capabilities and features, but I think it falls short of being as capable as I really need.  BTW, the other function a dashcam has is to save a brief video at the time of a collision, but I had no way to test this.

title: Good for versatility - sturdy - heavy - holds Pencil securely
text:
I was looking for something more like the smart keyboard that Apple makes, where it easily detaches but still has the case around the back. This does not quite fill that desire, but worth the price compared to the Apple brand.

The keyboard stays quite secure with a strong magnet behind it. While the keyboard is very light-weight, the magnet is very heavy, and this made me like it less (but since this is a personal preference, I still rated it with 5 stars as this may not bother other users).

I love how it holds the Pencil, but disappointed that it doesn't charge it on that side. It charges the Pencil, however, on the other side through the case very well, and when you flip it shut, if you forget about the pencil, the flap helps it so it doesn't get knocked off or lost in transit.

It folds around in many different positions, making it easy for me to leave the keyboard behind while I run around servicing technology around the school buildings I'm in, then I can flip it open to take quick notes with the Pencil. The iPad comes out easily enough that you could take it around with you without the whole case, but then you wouldn't have any protection. I was sort of hoping for a way to put a pop-socket on the case I got, but can't with this design.

If the keyboard "Charge" light lights up when it needs to be charged, then the battery seems pretty good, since I sometimes forget to turn off the keyboard, but have not yet had it die on me or have it tell me it needs charging after having a couple of months, now. Maybe the 'charge' light only lets you know when it is charging. If so, it would be nice if it had a battery gauge to let you know when it is getting low. Maybe I should read the instructions. 😉

If someone would copy the Apple Smart keyboard and case at an affordable price, though, I would jump on it!

Depending on what you need a case to do, I would recommend this one.

title: Great quality, fantastic price!
text:
I purchased this monitor for my wife to use with her Alienware R17X4 laptop. She had broken a key on her keyboard but also wanted a little larger screen. So, I purchased a wireless keyboard and this monitor. She now uses the powerful Alienware laptop as a desktop with a larger display and a wireless, movable keyboard. She is a very happy camper.

Others have commented on the great graphics, thin design, and good quality build for a great price, so I won't repeat those details here. I will however point out a few tips:

1. At first, it seems the stand will not tilt. But it does! Grasp the stand firmly and then tilt the monitor back to the desired position. Note it does not tilt forward or side to side, but does tilt back (facing more upwards towards your eyes) which really helps in most settings.
2. If you don't get a signal, make sure you plugs the HDMI cable into the "HDMI out" port on your PC, not the "HDMI in" port. Duh. I had mine plugged into the wrong port until I found my reading glasses and saw the problem.
3. We changed three settings which you may want to also do if you have a laptop. First, we changed the display settings to choose between "Second screen only", "Duplicate", or "Extend". We chose "Extend" so she can have two documents open at once on the two monitors, her laptop screen and the new monitor. You just drag one document off the edge of the monitor to move it to the other screen.
4. Next, we found that closing the laptop, when she only needed one screen, put it into hibernation and shut everything down. We went into Control Panel and changed Power Settings under "What happens when you close the lid". We changed it from "Hibernate" to "Do nothing". Now the laptop keeps running even when the laptop is closed.
5. Third, most Windows laptops are configured so you have to drag things off the right edge of your new remote monitor to get them onto the laptop screen. However we wanted her laptop setting to the left of her new monitor, so it was confusing to have to drag something off the right-hand edge of the monitor to get it onto the left-hand screen on the laptop. We went back into display settings, where you can drag the two monitors in the settings to reverse them. Now, she can drag items from the left-hand screen to the right-hand screen by dragging them in that direction, and vice versa. Much more intuitive to use that way.

With those changes to the settings, she can open the laptop and use it as two monitors, dragging and dropping documents and apps from one screen to another. When she closes the laptop lid, it reverts to a single monitor (the new Acer) but does not go to sleep. This is perfect for what she needs. She can still power off the monitor when not needed for an extended period. Also, the laptop speakers still work when she turns on the sound even when the laptop is closed.

I highly recommend this monitor for anyone wanting a very good quality, cost-effective solution.

title: Blue Screen of Death on a 2015 Camry
text:
For some reason, this exact same product listing has been discontinued elsewhere on Amazon. So, copy/pasting here.

Really wanted to preserve the original look of my car and liked the idea of a hidden module. The physical install process was actually very easy (though I got a printed sheet which was very high level, there are YouTube tutorials out there for other decks which are helpful).

Getting the thing working, however, was about three hours of formatting, resets, and factory restarts. Once everything was connected, things worked smoothly in the normal Toyota part of the car. I followed the instructions to set up the CARabc device exactly, and voila! Apple CarPlay magically appears. I wanted to see what the path was from my home screen to CarPlay, so I backed out of everything. And when I followed the directions to launch CarPlay, all I got was a blue screen. I gave it about 90 seconds, thinking it might be a boot issue, but nothing changes. I pulled everything apart, checked my connections, and tried again.

I tried plugging my phone directly into the device (required if you want to have wired connections to your phone, but otherwise optional) and got the same problem. I tried changing modes, screen resolution, means of access. I tried using the voice assistant button and hey! Voice assistant doesn't work anymore but it automatically launched CarPlay (I'm assuming it biased to launch Siri versus the Toyota one). Thinking I'll take the win for a haptic button versus a feature I don't even use, I take the win.

Again, I back out to try and repro the path to launch CarPlay. I didn't have everything put together and tied down, and wanted to ensure I had everything functioning. Aaaand, blue screen.

During this whole install, I'm listening to a podcast, and the car picks it up while I'm on the blue screen. Curious, I try tapping on the screen and it launches another podcast. Now I know that the issue is not that CarPlay doesn't work, but that the video firmware is struggling or incompatible.

Unfortunately, CARabc doesn't include a customer service number, FAQ page, or YouTube tutorial, but Amazon weirdly does. I explain exactly what I just explained here, and they go "here's a refund."

title: A great idea, but…
text:
This case could be great, but for a high end build, it’s not. If you are throwing prosumer parts together without much thought, it’s going to be fine.

The problems start when you want to take advantage of the design. The vertical GPU mount is poorly designed. It’s flimsy and the riser isn’t long enough. High end cards aren’t served well for both reasons, they waggle on the vertical hanging mount and that stresses the already stressed connection even more. The tight space also requires a sharp bend and the bear metal cutouts and soft/flimsy rubber insert can rain havoc on the riser, chewing it up around the connector. The flimsy hanging position makes water cooling the card with hard lines very risky, as it’s not secure.

Using the side space behind a vertical GPU seems like a no brainer, but the tilt out back plate also rules out hard lines on a radiator and soft lines push on the already flimsy hanging card while tilting out the back plate. In fairness, the instruction say to install the swinging hard plate with a GPU. But the hard plate swings too, and the securing bracket attaches to it, which makes accessing your DisplayPort cables a partial case disassembly that stresses hard lines too much, and the riser. It’s too jenky to use with good stuff. It’s for beginners with an old, cheap, small, air cooled card. So I don’t recommend a hanging GPU which is the reason I bought the case. Frankly this feature is extremely poorly implemented and extremely dangerous for hard line users.

I tried to use the 600 mm Thermaltake cable to hide it behind the motherboard. It is long enough, but the case design forces an upper PSU mount and the twists required make the vertical mount even trickier. That cable has every delicate leads near the card connector, which easily break when stressed. It’s doable, but give yourself an extra week to experiment slowly and carefully or you’ll ruin the card and the riser. Not good. You’ll also need an M2 only storage solution since the riser and PSU eliminate all extra drive space. High end builders probably do that anyway.

I did a hanging GPU with a custom mount using a combo of hardline and mostly hidden soft tubing. I had to disassemble everything several times for various case design flaws, like the need to remove a bottom mount radiator to run a hidden riser, and the need to remove the invertible bottom plate to drill holes for a rear mounted pump, which is tricky to fit given the riser is twisted back there, both underneath the PSU, which then puts its modular connectors into a metal cable mtg wall that must be disassembled and removed.

The front glass is fine for my airflow needs since I custom built a replacement GPU mount and the tilt out backplate to allow side fans and a thin 360 mm thin rad. But the case fought me, and the water loop, every step of the way. Almost any side-open case would have been a better starting point.

Using the mesh front option would be nice, but it must be fans-only to fit a 360mm on top or bottom, unless you possibly use two fans in the middle. So what’s the point? Ugly, poor design.

General quality is mediocre, as screws strip easily, the inversion plate hangs up on the cheap, half inserted screws trying to slide in its slots, which you need to take off even for a standard build to remove the badly placed cable mgt brackets and modular mounts, and all are flimsy.

Overall, I toyed with giving the EVO a 1-star review, but it’s probably a great case for low end, amateur, prosumer crap like store bought AIOs, 240 mm needs, and ugly front-center cables, riser cables, and uneven twisted soft lines and cables.

High end builders will want to avoid this minefield of bad design and low quality for risk of losing $7-$10K of quality parts to a flimsy, overly complex $50 case.

The glowing video reviews are aimed and simple builds with cheap stuff and should be viewed in that light. Anything interesting or expensive is risky and frustrating - chose almost any other case.

title: Good value for a TV!
text:
Originally I purchased the 720p version of this TV sold here, because my old 10+ year 720p store brand TV I bought from Best Buy so long ago finally gave out. I actually really liked that TV and it worked well for a desktop PC that I rarely use. I figured I didn't need to splurge for the 1080p version of this TV since the smaller resolution was perfectly fine for the few times I use my desktop PC. Unfortunately I realized when I hooked up the 720p version, the PC's resolution was actually 1080p, and it was showing through a 720p monitor... long story short, it looked very bad and I realized I had to return it and splurge for the 1080p option. Quick review of the 720p one: Great quality overall, I actually really liked the viewing angles and picture quality of that. I think it would make for a great TV, however for a PC it made the text a bit choppy and difficult to read, so I don't recommend it as that. The same day, I went and ordered this 1080p version. It is designed slightly differently but overall looks the same. Resolution is much better, makes everything on my PC look normal again. I am pretty disappointed with the viewing angles and brightness. The TV is almost darker around the edges. It almost looks like it fades into the edges, which is very strange. Viewing angles are atrocious, but part of that could be attributed to the strange darkness around the edges. Screen is pretty bright, in general for a budget TV I'm happy. But oddly enough the screen on my very old TV that I was using before almost seemed better. Let's just hope I get another 10+ years use out of this one!

The setup was very, very easy. It tries to make you register for a Roku account however look carefully at all your options, you can choose to ignore the setup (it was completely unnecessary for me) and go straight to using it as a computer monitor. The setup however is pretty easy and self explanatory. The "smart" aspect of this TV works well, it's not laggy at all like other smart TVs I have (though they are older as well). I would totally suggest getting this if you plan on using it as an actual TV. As a PC monitor it's alright, but I can't help but feel like since you're looking at it closer up when as a PC monitor, it might be better to spend a little more for a better brand with a better quality panel. This here gets the job done but I'm not wowed. Another pro is that it is VERY, very light. I was shocked at how light it was. Definitely not what I'm used to from my older flat screen TVs!

title: Makes my 99 4runner look more like an 09.
text:
Works as advertised. The hardest part was running the wires. Here's basically how I hooked it up. Remove door paneling/kick plates where you are going to run the wires. Attach license plate frame camera. Remove the left license plate light and ran the wires into the lift gate. From the back of the lift gate, ran the wires through the rubber boot on the top left. (This part was a little tricky. I used an electrician's fish tape. ) This got my wires inside the 4Runner to the entry point near the rear dome light.

At this point, the included wire for the positive and negative leads on the power ran out, so I used my own 20 gauge hookup wire. The negative lead I connected to a common ground that my taillights were using. The positive lead I ran along the factory wire harness on the left (easy to see once the panel and kick plates are removed) and connected to the reverse wire in the back of my head unit. I also ran the video wire like this too. The I ran another short wire connecting the 4runner reverse light (red and blue wire on 99 4runner) to the positive lead going back to the head unit. I used quick-splice connections for this. Put the door panels back/license plate light/kick panels back on, and you are good to go.

So now, when I put the car into reverse, the reverse light comes on, gives power to the camera and the radio knows I'm in reverse, and switches to the camera view.

Took about a couple of hours. If you don't want to mess with running wires, you might want to get the wireless transmitter. My only grip was with the wires for the power. They seem very fragile, and could have been a little longer.

title: Working Fine in My Install
text:
This product installs in a fairly straightforward manner if one possesses a few basic skills. It was necessary to drill a hole through my vehicle's skin behind the license plate in order to fish the video and power cable into the interior of the end gate. I used an ample amount of silicone sealant to ensure the install would remain will required fishing a longer cable up through the end gate, through the tubular rubber "chase" to access the vehicle body, over the headliner and down the A pillar to get the video into the front cabin under the dash. I did replace the RCA video cable supplied with the product with a Steren 25' Python Home Theater RCA-RCA Video Cable, also available from Amazon, because I wanted a heavier-duty cable that would withstand the abrasion of fishing through tight spaces in the vehicle and also would not likely present issues of degradation image quality due to the length of the run, though it's reasonable to presume that Esky has provided one of sufficient quality to provide adequate video quality, albeit somewhat flimsy and not likely to be so resilient to physical abrasion.

The power cable run was not complicated. In my vehicle, the backup light is in the end gate. It's necessary to remove all the interior trim pieces so as to be able to get into the end gate. The power and ground wires were readily identifiable once that was accomplished. In my case, in a 2013 Ford Escape, the positive wire to the reversing light is blue and the negative ground is black. I simply stripped off some of the insulation on both, wrapped the appropriate wire from the camera around it and then soldered the connections, after which I insulated them well with electrical tape. I also took some care to tape the entire assembly to another cable in the area so as to prevent the weight of the cabling combined with vehicle vibration to potentially cause a separation or other issue over time. In my particular installation, the trim went back on easily. There are several clips that, with some care taken to achieve proper alignment, allow everything to go back on without much trouble.

The camera produces a clear image and there is a grid that delineates the distance quite well. The camera can be positioned up and down by loosening a setscrew and then retightening after adjustment. In my case, I did it without assistance, so the process required two such repositioning attempts to get it exactly where I wanted. That wasn't much of a task.

I've had the installation in place about a month now and, thus far, it's saved me from at least one situation where a car was backing out of a parking space immediately behind me on the other side of a parking lot travel lane and I did anticipate a person with a shopping cart so as to stop a little sooner than I might otherwise have done without its benefit.

Additionally, I would say this: The camera is a good augmentation to other existing safety devices, as well as one's own faculties. There is a bit of a learning curve to integrate the camera image into one's usual backing routine. It's important to remember that there are rear view mirrors on one's vehicle and that they are there for a purpose, so one should be mindful of them and utilize them with which to back up as safely as possible. If one should become solely dependent on this backup camera, ignoring the other available options, there is a significant risk that safety will actually be degraded as a result, especially for pedestrians in a parking lot. It's also important to realize that, if a driver is ignoring caution in a parking lot, he or she may approach one's vehicle from the side at relatively high speed, and this device isn't likely to provide an advantage in anticipating that situation, so it's best to be looking around as one proceeds in reverse as well. Even though this camera has a fairly wide angle of view, it does not supplant the driver's faculties, such as turning one's head to each side of the vehicle to observe any potential oncoming vehicles to the right and left, especially in a parking lot situation, or the use of outside mirrors to increase the field of view. However, for people and objects that may be positioned directly behind one's vehicle, especially if one's vehicle limits visibility directly behind due to a high rear window position, such as mine, this camera can augment other means of viewing the area into which one may intend to back up. It's just not a panacea for all backup situations and should not be relied upon exclusively. It certainly doesn't hurt to turn one's head around side-to-side to be certain one has all the information possible before and during a reversing maneuver. Good luck and safe driving.

I didnt even get to turn on the laptop more than once before a problem occurred. I dont really have high hopes for this laptop for the future. It's a good thing I wanted a laptop for seldom uses otherwise I would have been upset to be stuck with such a device.

title: Great Hybrid Watch!! Practical & Stylish!
text: Definitely a good watch that exceeded my expectations! Granted, this watch may NOT work for everyone. I have had the basic smartwatches and in truth didn't care for them because they all look too cartoonish for a mature adult. (just my opinion) While I am a techie guy I am more inclined towards gadgets & products that are practical for what I use....for example I don't need to talk into my watch for a phone call when I have Bluetooth earbuds in 90% of the time....nor do I need to be able to try and text with watch face since most of my texts are received text to voice with earbuds and voice to text for responses. Having just the ability to read the notice of text on watch face is all needed to determine if response is urgent or not. This watch is great for those that fall in the middle when it comes to tech gadgets!! It is stylish enough to wear both with casual attire and dressy attire. It enables all my gym work outs to be monitored and recorded with heart rate, daily steps, distance walked, SP02, etc. integrating great into my google fit app. It measures blood oxygen level pretty accurately. Can control my music without having to grab phone. Weather information on watch face when needed with Alexa for request of even more detailed weather report requests. Easily add things to all my lists and calendar on Alexa (i.e. to-do, grocery, reminders, etc.) Notifications of email showing subject line, texts showing opening sentence of text (most times all of short texted messages) All my alerts and notifications of majority of my phone apps such as alarm system notices, camera surveillance notices, FB, Instagram, Twitter, flight notices, calendar notices, reminders appear on the watch face with a moderate vibrate for the alert --  apps are customizable for which ever apps you want push notices displayed on watch in real time. So with all this good stuff I am perfectly content and need nothing more....If you prefer android, google services, and amazon Alexa services this is the watch for you as it works seamlessly with these so far from my experience with my watch. The Fossil App was super easy to pair to set up the watch. Syncing thus far has been automatic with no issues.  -- Now for the drawbacks -- while you have lots of customizable watch faces to choose from the dark background ones can be difficult to see in poor lighting although there is the option to turn back light on as needed. There is no speaker on watch so sound is not an option for music or phone conversations however a microphone exists and works perfectly with Alexa. Alexa responds with onscreen text on the watch face. -- Vibrate notices along with onscreen detailed notices work just fine for me! -- The perhaps biggest draw back is your phone MUST be within a reasonable range for full functionality, Bluetooth connection, and syncing. For me this isn't an issue as my phone is always in my briefcase/luggage nearby or my pocket depending on my activities. Hopefully this helps others with some of the things I wanted to know before I purchased the watch. I have been a fan of fossil watches and as always this watch didn't disappoint! Definitely would recommend and purchase again in future.

title: Good for gaming, bad for productivity
text:
First. Yes, HDR does in fact work. I've tried on numerous games and videos now. Unfortunately, this doesn't mean there aren't problems with this monitor.

The monitor has two major faults though. First, it's very expensive. Arguably too expensive since it's a bit of a one trick pony. Why? The second fault; the FALD mini led pattern is visible against solid backgrounds depending on the color and brightness. This apparently varies from unit to unit and is unfortunately a bit of a lottery. This is not unique to this monitor, you can search Google for several TVs and other FALD monitors that have this issue. Just how visible it is varies across all panels. That's a bad spot to be in. For everyone. Lots of RMAs. Lots of money. Lots of time. Lots of feels.

The good news is the FALD grid pattern is mostly invisible in games and video content. The bad news is it can be seen against white background sometimes which is one of the worst colors for it as so many applications and web sites have white backgrounds. My unit became seemingly worse over time + you can see the pattern. It eventually becomes too distracting. It's yellow against white. Not gray on white, no, it's yellow! Makes it harder to ignore. Some also call this the dirty screen effect (DSE).

This can utterly destroy the monitor's usefulness for productivity use.

If this doesn't bother you and your unit doesn't have any dead pixels, loud popping noises from heat, etc. Congrats! You have the best (or one of) ultrawide gaming monitor on the market. Certainly the best 32:9.

Samsung (CSOT) better get a handle on its quantum dot transfer process and ensure that grid pattern is not visible. They do that and they absolutely will hold the lead here. Once the HDR confusion goes away, this will likely be the biggest complaint from people and biggest issue this panel will face. I'm sure there's some unaffected panels out there...but I don't think the odds of finding one is very high unfortunately. I wanted to love this monitor.

title: A Tornado -- Good and Bad!
text:
Does this thing blow? You bet! But after years of using "canned air," the accompanying factors sort of took me by surprise.

Unlike using air cans, with which you can precisely pulse and control the air output, using this device is more like firing up a coffee pot-sized tornado. Oh, it cleans, but it's also like unleashing a small jet engine. It spools up and it spools down, and there's no real trigger. It's on -- FULL BLAST -- or it's off.

I had stuff flying around my office, calendars fell off the wall, stuff being blown off my desk and falling behind the desk, and general craziness ensued. :) And that was just the first time...

This awesome tool requires technique. Just keep that in mind. It's probably better to take the device to be cleaned to the "blast" area rather than trying to "blast" a device in its native surroundings.

Oh -- and buy the "ugly" color and save $10. It's the same device in every way but color.

I love this device...but I clearly need to figure out how to best use it. :)

The battery life has been good as well. Oh, and I can talk thru them. It must be clear because when I call out a chicken's name, she turns towards the camera to look for me. I've been through quite a number of products with these chickens as I've learned what worked well and what different. For cameras, this is it for me. title: Plex Server Dream or Nightmare 'Linux Mint Mate 18.3'
text:
Picked up the PCIE version of the TP-Link Gigabit Ethernet not realizing it used the Realtek drivers that could be a problem on Linux. I was setting up a Plex Server on Linux Mint Mate 18.3 with old parts laying around needing only a Mainboard and Case. The built in GLAN network on budget Mainboard was giving me shut down problems, Catch 22 took over as soon as I installed this card, as it used the same r8169 driver causing the shut down problems. Found the needed info to get it working online for Blacklisting the r8169 driver and compiling the r8168 driver to cure the restart/shut down problem. With that problem out of the way the card works a bit better than the onboard GLAN that needed the same compiled driver.

Getting 87mB/s to 92mB/s file share uploads to Linux Mint Mate 18.3 Plex Server, Restarts and shut downs no longer a problem. All in all good card that Linux isn't set to work cleanly without some extra steps.

title: Here’s What’s Missing On This “Has-It-All” (Almost) Surge Outlet
text:
Reason bought
I bought this for two (2) primary reasons, surge protection and ability to shut-off (to stop phantom power drain). I liked all the other bells and whistles; I won’t repeat what those are.

Almost is not the same as having it
The manufacturer tried make this a “has-it-all” device. But it fails for some very important reasons, when it comes down to the most basic of functions for this device. (1) It has no CSA/UL/ETL certifications and (2) its surge features.

Disappointed, here’s why.

• Not certified
• Unknown clamping voltage.

What we have
The joule rating is 1440. That’s nice. However, those who know better say the joule rating should, at minimum, be at least 1,000, and preferably 2,000. However, going well over 2,000 is strongly suggested, as in minimum 3,000, that is 1,000 per “leg” (i.e., prong) of that plug.

What it is
The joule rating is how much excess energy the device can withstand before frying. Once fried from a surge larger than its joule rating, it no long protects anything. In addition, to my understanding, the joule rating is also a type of measure of life span. Over time, your suppressor is going to take surge hits. The joule rating is also an indication of how long the suppressor will survive with all those hits - higher is better. To me, it’s like a bank account, being depleted over time, until all those joules are gone (spent) then that pin hole green light on the device no longer shows green. Get your magnifying glass out on occasion and see if that surge light is still on.

Only half the surge story
The joule rating is only half the surge story. The other half, and vital, is the pass-through voltage, also referred to as the clamping voltage, i.e., what I will refer to as the Voltage Protection Rating. The preference is to pass through a lower number of volts to what is plugged in. Think about it, your residence is built to supply your average household device 120 volts. So, let’s think about this. Say the power company throws a switch that causes a huge surge in voltage, say 500 volts. How many volts will this suppressor allow through to that fancy smart phone. Preferably, something a lot, lot less than 500 volts, to avoid your device getting fried.

What clamping voltage does this have?
Here, we have no idea what that clamp-down voltage is, i.e., what excess voltage this device will slam the door on after allowing a value higher than 120volts. Hmmmmm.

What no certifications?
Finally, this device has no certifications from any known agency, such as CSA/UL/ETL,
A certification isn't a requirement to sell an electronic device in the US. But do we really want to trust a device that the manufacturer did not want a third-party to certify? Typically, certifications are noted on the device, along with clamping voltage. We see nothing here.

Bottom-line:
We appreciate all the bells and whistles this device has, but it’s missing what we also want. Our fault for not really looking into this device before selecting. So, we will only take a star off, as everything else worked. But it’s a weak four (4) stars. We won’t select this again.

We hope our photos and thoughts assist in your decision.

title: Needs to be Formatted. Why? How?
text:
When I saw this flash drive, I knew I had to have it. The ability to transfer photos and files from computer to phone, back and forth, really appealed to me.

After plugging this into my iPhone, it immediately told me that I needed to go to the App Store and download a program called Y disk to transfer files.

Y disk is a terrible non-intuitive app that (at first) seems to only lets you copy 10 images at a time. With about 150 images for me to copy, it took me a while – until I discovered another way to copy a lot more images to the flash drive quickly.

Then I removed the flash drive and plugged it into my computer.

BIG PROBLEM.

I got a message telling me that I needed to format the drive before using it. And of course, I would lose all my data.

I started to quick-format it, but it would not allow quick formatting, so I used slow formatting. But that never worked. I tried with both exFAT and NTFS using many various allocation units, but nothing worked. In most cases it started to format. Some of the formatting options quit immediately, Most started for format for about 10 minutes before quitting. One lasted nearly an hour before it quit. But in all cases, it eventually gave ne the message that Windows can’t format it.

I understand this may not happen to everyone. Maybe it’s my computer itself that is having the problem formatting. But overall I now have this flash drive that is completely useless to me.

title: Amazing sound underwater!
text: These are amazing headphones! The sound is unbelievable! I only use them in MP3 mode for swimming laps, and as soon as I put my head in the water the sound is amazing! A couple of the songs I loaded have some  deep, pounding bass, and I swear I can feel tapping on my cheeks. But it doesn’t seem too loud. They are very comfortable to wear and I like that they fit around my neck instead of around my head. My previous pair had an adjustable silicone strap that was attached into the frame that would keep it firm to the back of your head.  Now the bad part: the buttons are unbelievably small and too close together. I turned the MP3 player off four or five times when I was trying to skip a song or adjust the volume. I could not feel the the different buttons! I hated that I had to stop swimming, take the headphones off and look at the buttons in order to change the song and/or volume. I mean I  HATED it! So I came up with a plan. I affixed little tiny seed beads on the buttons… two on the up button and one on the down button. I used resin and cured it with a UV lamp. Problem solved! Now I can feel the buttons and I haven’t turned the headset off once by accident. Yay!

title: Love it!
text:
I have a couple of these now. I absolutely love them and use them everyday. Sometimes I use more than one at the same time. There are a few specific features that are great:

* There is a drawer on the side. On this one, the drawer is also the handle so you wouldn't be able to keep stuff in there and it not fall out when moving it around. This hasn't been an issue for me personally though. I usually use the drawer for a place to put whatever I'm working on at the moment so it can be handy but out of the way. On this model the drawer is made so you can scoop out whatever is in there easily (my other one didn't have that and I thought it would be a good thing to add so I'm glad that they did). I really like how the drawer is located on the side rather than in front so you don't have to move your whole body to open it.

* There is a cup holder. I love how there is a little cup holder which is perfect for a place to put your drink so it doesn't leak anywhere but in the cup holder. It doesn't go down very far which is great for me. I often times use it for a place to collect my beads or little pieces I'm working with so they don't roll away. It is perfectly positioned towards the top left corner.

* There is a slot at the top. I think it's meant for a tablet or cell phone but I like it for my instructions or my pens. I also like how it has holes in the slot, It makes it easy to clean it with a rag because sometimes it will get crumbs in there and would otherwise be kind of hard to clean out.

* There is a handle to carry it. I like that it is open and easy to grab with your hand. It's also an opening to the drawer so I can put things in it if I need to and they collect in the drawer. Very handy.

* This one has 4 USB ports for charging things or to power the cute little fan and light that they give you too. It's very nice especially for doing my crafts. I've used it as an extention to charge my phone actually and have extra openings to charge other things.

* The legs fold out of the bottom. They are very easy to fold out and they have foam pads which are grippy so they don't slide around easily.

I find this table very useful. It looks nice and is well-made. They have taken the time to add little features to make life easier. I would highly recommend this to anyone. It's good for anything really and for anyone. Sometimes I sit on the floor with it and sometimes I put it on the bed with me. Sometimes I have it standing up and sometimes I just lay it flat on the floor or bed. I would give this a 10 out of 10 rating. I'm sure I will be purchasing more in the future. It's well worth the price.

title: checks all the boxes, reasonably priced
text:
What I needed:
-wireless keyboard w/touch pad
(I buy or keep old computers and use them as media hubs for TV's in my house)
-usb reciever
(as opposed to blutooth as I can hide said old computers and use a dongle for the receiver for better connection, and can turn the keyboard on and off without much connecting device delay)
-backlit
(So I can watch movies in low light settings but still use the keyboard)

There are three keyboards I have found and purchased that fulfill this criteria: the Rii K18 Plus Wireless, the Logitech K830, and the Coastacloud 2.4G Wireless TV Keyboard

The TLDR: of this is that I think the Coastacloud is the best value for the money, the Logitech is the best but most expensive, and while the Rii had many good things at such a low price-point it had one design choice that would stop me from buying it personally again. Specifically not having mouse keys by the touchpad but instead having mouse zones. Dragging and dropping or grabbing the scroll bar was always an inconvenience with the Rii.

at only about $14 more than the Rii, with a much longer battery life, proper mouse keys, volume keys (the rii required pressing the function key to change the volume), more colors, a more solid chicklit keybaord (the Rii had rubber keycaps on a membrane board that lacked tactile responsiveness), more backlight color options, as well as backlight intensity options,and a few other quality of life features the Coastacloud is definitely worth the extra money.

Really the only things that puts the logitech keyboard ahead of the coastacloud is the build quality and the logitech support/bios software which allow for more customization (although notably not available for mac OS's). The Logitech keyboard touchpad feels more responsive, battery is bigger and longer lasting and having a mouse button accessible for the left hand is a nice touch. But at roughly $20 more than the Coastacloud, and about $60-$65 for a keyboard when on sale, I feel like the price jump vs quality and usability is less of a value gain than the jump from the Rii to the coastacloud.

Ultimately I'd consider buying the Logitech again if it was on sale when i needed another keybaord as the price difference is closer to $10-$15 than the potential $60 when it is not on sale (perhaps for a living room setup), but after a few weeks of usage I am very satisfied with the coastacloud and I think it is definitely the best value for the money.

title: Small package, big sound
text:
This little Bluetooth speaker is both the smallest, and has the best sound, of the many I’ve tried in search of decent sound. This one is the winner for me.
I included a shot of the speaker sitting on an iPhones 13 pro max, to get an idea of its compact size.
The sound is surprisingly crisp and clear, and as other reviewers have shown, it’s actually waterproof.
Pairing and streaming music has been easy and seamless.
Speaker has a TF/micro SD slot so it can be a stand alone unit that can play your playlist without the need to pair with the phone.
It has a rubber base that keeps it from sliding around, or it has a loop you can hang it from.
The light on the end pulses to the music in 3 settings including shutting that feature off altogether.
Bluetooth range is decent unobstructed but I had trouble keeping the signal if the phone moved with me to a different floor in the house but that isn’t a concern for me.
A couple quirks: it plays an absolutely comical power up and power down sound sequence. It has an associated app, completely in a non-English language. I’d probably stay away from that.

Quality of sound for the size makes this speaker worth any quirks.

title: Sound Quality is Great, Build is Great, Design is Good to Great, Mic is Decent Enough
text:
Shipped very quickly. Thank you! The sound quality is pristine, provided you can find a static-free station in your area. I don't find the bass boost function useful for every song, but in cases where it does improve the song, you can simply push the button to use it. Nice!

The Bluetooth connectivity is lightning fast. I connected to it right away. Because my car has two 12V ports (yes, that's not normal), I was able to set it up on the one on the left, then wanted to move it to the right one and as soon as I did, my phone was immediately connected again with no effort and in a mere split second. That's a far cry from what I'm used to. The mics work well enough. I tested this with someone else and they said it sounded like I was in a box, but it was clear. They said my phone's hands-free calling sounded better, but both were clear. Also, because my car has an Aux port (think of it like a headphone jack), I can connect this to the Aux port for static free play, while my phone is connected to this device via bluetooth. Yay!

The device is feature-rich. Quick Charge (QC) 3.0, a supposed 40+W charging capability and USB-C all make for a nice set of options not usually all found on one device. I haven't tested the charging capability yet, so I'll have to update my review later. As far as the lighting, it's simply just rainbow. If that's not your thing, you can turn it off. The lit LED display easily shows the station it's tuned to, car battery charge (when you plug it in or the car turns on) and the volume. The knob works for volume adjustment, calls and play/pause. There is a button rocker on the right side that allows you to do previous/next song. The bass boost is a nice thing to have at your fingertips when you want it. It says you can even put songs on a thumb drive and plug it into it and play your songs that way. The built-in mics can work for hands-free calls.

For the price, I highly recommend this bluetooth adapter.

A few things I would have preferred are:

1) LED light colors other than just rainbow
2) Perhaps less bulky
3) A fast-forward/rewind function (perhaps a push-twist or shift the knob left/right?)

title: Anytime earbuds claim "deep bass" be skeptical - Not great fit, not PS5 compatible
text:
These earbuds have a lot of flash going on, but in terms of user experience that's where they stop impressing and start underwhelming.

First off, what's good:
1. Pairing.
Bluetooth pairing has come a long way in the last decade and now instead of crossing your fingers and hoping your device and your headphones/speakers will show up when you ask them to look for each other, it's much easier. Sure enough, when you take these out of their case and they launch into "discoverable" mode, it's a small matter of just selecting them from your device's bluetooth options, and you're good to go.

Quick note here: I'd picked these up in the off-hand chance that maybe, JUST MAYBE, they'd pair and work with the PS5 as a wireless headphone and mic combo. ***THEY DO NOT WORK w/ PS5***. I'm putting that in caps not because it's a serious flaw, I 90% expected they wouldn't, but a man can dream. I just want to get that out of the way in case anyone else was wondering/hoping also. I don't even consider that a strike against the product.

2. Battery life.

Look, anytime Bluetooth is involved, I know battery life is going to take a hit. Bluetooth is a battery vampire, but we put up with it because, hey, not having a headphone cord scraping across your collar and sending noise up to the earpieces is really, really nice. In my uses of these headphones, they've been lasting through the days when I use them as long as I make sure to put them back in the case between uses instead of just taking them out and putting them in my pocket forgetting they're still linked to my device. That's probably the worst mistake you can make if you want your headphones and your device to have power at the end pf the day.

3. Sound quality.

Okay, so I'm separating Sound Quality and Bass Quality, because while these things DO NOT deliver on bass like they claim to, as far as just providing good clean sound for music and making phone calls or watching a show or movie on your device, these are perfectly capable and stuff sounds pretty good with a nice field of depth for earbuds.

And now, what's not so good.

1. The attempt at tapping/hands-free controlling on the earbuds.

Yeah, good luck with that. Half the time I attempted to control my device's volume/mic control/next-prev track/etc. whatever else these things promise to do with taps and swipes, the tactile sensing of the earpieces is just so finnicky and hard to pindown that's it's not really worth it. If that's a factor that weighs heavily into what you want from bluetooth headphones, don't bother with these. For me, it was less of an issue because I still operate from a "prefer to be looking at my device when I'm using it" mindset, so it's usually open/unlocked in front of me anyways. For volume, I rely more on the side buttons of my phone than I do trying to tap my earbuds.

2. Bass Quality

I'm sorry, but these things do not have good bass and it's weird that tried to single that out as something they bring to the table over other headphones. And this isn't even a case of comparing apples to oranges, because yes, if you REALLY care about bass, you're going to invest in some studio headphones and go that route, but even with other earbuds I've had many do bass better than these. When these things encounter deep bass they do what many earbuds do and end up trying to digitally imitate it and you end up with distortion. This is a pretty common thing with earbuds, and frankly it's not surprising that these things suffer the same problem. What's surprising was that they tried to brand themselves as being GOOD at bass. They're earbuds, drawing attention to how they handle bass is not a good idea.

3. Ear fit and feel

This is always a very, very subjective game of comfort roulette anytime you have earbuds with completely solid earpieces made to go inside the ear. Every ear is not shaped the same, so for some, these will be a perfect fit and they'll be confident enough to even go jogging with them in. For me, that's not the case. For me these stay in well enough for casual listening and viewing, but anything too movement intensive and these things get jostled out. Honestly, if these would have had the kind of buds with silicone pieces that fit into the ear that would've helped immensely, but I get it, they wanted to go for the iPhone earbud style imitation. But for me, that style of earbud has always been a bit uncomfortable and problematic in terms of fit.

4. The charging light patterns/color scheme

This is a minor thing, and the instructions clear this up, but the choice to go with solid red as the "charging is done" indicator color is counterintuitive to me.

title: So Far So Good
text:
I unboxed it this morning to get this review written. Here's the short version:

Pros (in order of importance to this gal):

High air pressure
Compact
Lightweight
Portable
Numerous attachments for vacuuming and blowing
Parts are simple and easy to insert and remove
Extra filters of each type (Yes!)

Cons (same order as Pros):

Short cord
Blown air is hot
Blowing instructions need refinement
Hose position has to be swapped for vacuuming or blowing
Filters have to be removed or added for vacuuming or blowing
Hose is troublesome to store

The longer version for those who like more detail.

The instructions for the vacuum have their own section and are thorough. The instructions for the blower are kind of tossed into the general instructions. Not a deal breaker, but having a different section for the vacuum and not for the blower piqued my technical writing urge to edit the booklet. A simple change from "Operation" to "Air Blower Operation" would fix that, and number 1 is to plug the unit in. That instruction should be moved to After the unit is prepped for air blowing - best to remove and add things while the unit is unplugged. Read the instructions in reverse and it's good. Fortunately there is a diagram of the unit with labels for each piece and part as well as a set of cleaning instructions with diagrams picturing each filter. With those diagrams it was easy enough to decipher the air blowing instructions and I only doubt my set up because the air is so warm.

The air coming out is about the equivalent of a hair dryer set on normal. Not a great thing for computer parts, which should be kept at low temps; however, a computer Should be off when cleaning it out.

The power cord is maybe 24" long so an extension cord may be needed. We take our computers outside for cleanings so we'll definitely need an extension.

The hose is also about 24" and it has a connection that stays in place while the hose is being screwed in so the hose doesn't flop all over the place - excellent feature. A tie of some sort would have been good to include in the package to keep it together for storage. It's separate from the machine because you'll have to attach it to the front for blowing and the back for vacuuming. It doesn't coil up, which is helpful for the purpose of vacuuming or blowing, but a detriment when it comes to storage.

Storage - I'm unsure if the bag is intended to house the hose or the unit. The instruction booklet indicates, "The provided black bag is used to pack the nozzles, excluding the electric duster." However, there are a few errors throughout the booklet (do not vacuum the water) so I'm not entirely sure it didn't mean to say Including. The bag is Quite large for just nozzles.

The nozzles are fantastic. I was able to get into nooks and crannies that have been collecting dust for ages and the nastiness came right on out. I can't wait to get out there and tackle my car!

Everything is easy to remove and put back in, even with my arthritic hands. The unit has a carrying handle and the cord wraps around that. The hose is the only awkward thing about it. It's interesting how exciting it was to find an additional set of filters - no one does that! This means while one set is drying, the work can continue. Or, if you have a users who will be sharing this who Never clean the filters (as I do), you can have "Mine" and "Theirs" filters. :D

All-in-all the cons are minor inconveniences, save for the cord. The cord is a sticking point for me. I understand it should be short to keep the unit's bulk to a minimum, but it's going to be a pain to go get the extension cord each time I need to use this. Never having to pay for another freezing can of air that's lost pressure, though, supersedes that inconvenience.

title: Super-sweet front-facing bike light for Garmin users
text:
What a great concept from Clevermen -- a front light that fits underneath your Garmin bike computer.
It is astounding that it took this long for someone to offer such a light, but Clevermen have done a good job of offering a near perfect solution.

Over the years, I have bought and tried countless front lights as I have noticed that a higher percentage of cars see and account for me, especially cars turning across my lane in front. Out of all these trials, each light I've tried has failed until the Cleverman FR160. There are a multitude of issues that I've encountered, namely they take up too much space on my handlebar, the battery is too small for medium to long rides, the charging port is inconvenient and/or an old USB port. Many of them are too bulky or use AAA or AA batteries that make them overlarge. The list goes on and on.

So Clevermen with the FR160 have come up with a light that fits underneath my Garmin, so it takes no handlebar space at all, is easy to charge with a USB C port, lasts long enough for an average 50 mile ride and has good visibility from the front and sides.

Just on the basis of all these critical plus points I'm giving it the full 5 stars -- no question about it.

That being said, I do see things that could be added to edge it closer to perfection. The easiest would be to move the on/off switch on one side or the other instead of having it at the back. Since the Garmin overhangs the light quite a bit it is hard to turn the light on and off at the half-way coffee stop. The same is true of the USB port when charging at home. I leave the two devices connected at all times, so it would be more convenient to have both the on/off and USB port on the side.

Another improvement would be to have the light contain a gyro option so it turns itself on and off when it detects movement. It would also be great if the light would talk to my Garmin so that various options could be setup and the battery level displayed on the screen of the Garmin.

These are all nice-to-have suggestions and do not detract from the great job Clevermen have done to bring this light to market. I will say that it seems a little pricey, but at the same time, I feel that the combination of features make it well worth the cost -- so much so that I do not want to ride without it.
