title: Handy Cassette Converter
text:
I was a bit skeptical when I ordered this, since, for what it purported to do, the price was very low. I have a lot of music on cassettes that I want to convert to MP3s, but haven't gotten around to it until now. I can attest that this little tape player gets the job done. I popped the cassettes in and let the player do its thing (transferring the songs into MP3 files on the USB flash drive). It did that very smoothly, although since most of my tapes are homemade, the player could not detect the song breaks, so after I plugged the recorded flash drive into my computer, I had to install the breaks myself. A little time-consuming but not a deal-breaker. I now have the songs digitally preserved and can play them on multiple devices. No worries about cassettes wearing out or breaking and losing the music.

While this little guy will play cassettes on its own, the player has no speaker or Bluetooth connectivity, so one has to use wired earbuds or hook it up to separate speaker. Since the battery compartment for the AA batteries is under the cassette compartment itself and only last for two hours, it is not practical to use this as a Walkman-like player while walking around, since to put in new batteries requires taking out the cassette first. Over the headphones the music on the cassettes sounds fine, but I would not buy this unit just to listen to old cassettes. There are many better options for that out there. For converting old tapes to MP3s, however, this works well and the price is hard to beat.

My one complaint about this player is the look and labelling of the control buttons. Even with my reading glasses it is hard to see the markings on the buttons to know which one to press. I had to refer a number of times to the instruction paper to figure out which button was which. In addition, some of the buttons are really tiny and,, to my mind anyway not laid out intuitively. That having been said, I was able to eventually figure out which button was which and now can use the player easily. So far, I am pleased with this acquisition.

title: Great Sound Quality, Wonky Charging
text:
I've had a long and varied experience with the Ankbit E500Pro Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Headphones. I ordered them this summer to bring on some travels; the wired aspect of the headphones was appealing for the plane, and I used them wired in the beginning exclusively.

When we returned home I tried using them wirelessly and at first they were like a dream. The sound really is good and being wireless is so much more convenient. When their battery ran out I charged them. Or, I should say, I tried charging them. They wouldn't take the charge. I tried every variation I could come up with when plugging them in to charge but they just wouldn't charge.

I contacted the manufacturer and they immediately sent me a replacement pair of headphones. I had the same issue with the second pair. At this point in time I'm thinking "what am I doing wrong??!" but didn't get any troubleshooting from the manufacturer, so I don't know. I've read and reread the directions multiple times. I believe I'm following the directions for charging.

The second pair of headphones takes a charge, sometimes. It's wonky. They sometimes will be charged and last for hours and other times won't even turn on after "charging".

I've taken off only one star for these otherwise exceptional headphones because I'm still not convinced there's some degree of user error going on here. I wish I knew for sure. Great sound, nice noise canceling feature (it really does work! These are my first noise canceling headphones and the difference when you turn on the noise canceling option is awesome). Hopefully my experience is an anomoly.

text:
I think all the reviews here speak for themselves so I will keep mine brief. First I bought a 43 inch, but it was too big till I get moved, so I came back and got the 32 inch, think I paid 129.00 ish? That was for the 1080p. This (these) were my first SMART TVs. I was worried about it, everything so techy esp. to us older, set in our ways people.

Set up was SUPER EASY, picture quality AWESOME, sound GREAT (I mean some might like a soundbar) but for me it has enough range and base for me to be VERY impressed compared to other TVs I own. Can set the volume lowish and its still quite loud and clear and balanced. Getting ROKU set up was easy and a WHOLE NEW world opened before me, streaming! Then I got brave and opted to -sort of- cut the cord, bye bye TV cable boxes, I just use the cable app and an antenna for local. That saved near 90 bucks off by cable bill. YAY!

Never could I say a TV was life changing but for me, these (I got 2) were! I came back to get another for a back bedroom and I see they are sold out and only with secondary sellers who have jacked up the price over 100.00 in all cases. Nope. I was sad. But off to Walmart.com I went and I got another even CHEAPER than here, for $119.00 for a 32 inch.

PRICE and QUALITY and teaching an old person to stream headache free for the first time in my life, FANTASTIC! But do NOT buy here from these secondary make a profit sellers. WAAAAY OVERPRICED from Amazon's original pricing! (I just bought a few months ago). Go to Walmart online!

The only thing I still can't move past and don't like, is no numbers on the remote. I also have my phone as a remote too which is neat, but it's hard letting go of numbers when watching cable app. I guess I will adjust.

title: You get what you pay for so buy 2!
text:
It's true, unless you are buying a big label brand of even a t-shirt, you get what you pay for. And the value here is just ridiculous! Let us all be sure to set expectations properly.

The 'CupeISI' 10.1 Inc Quad-Core 64GB Android Tablet is quite the value buy.
This is running Android 11, functional but saw no way to upgrade. Don’t panic, 11 was released in 2020 and still has security support and patching.

We are using this as a home automation/monitoring cameras in the house type tablet and one of the apps is going to need tinkering to work but may not be supported.
Just be sure to check your use case and app load for sure (or if running Android 11 on your phone then you are good to go here with any app on there).

Don't take this to the concert or sunset for taking pictures, it has a camera, but didn't expect even mild quality, but may I remind you the price.

We tested some games, once you get there, it's fine, just takes longer to load or swap between challenges or races etc.
The resolution is 1280x800: Basically 720p.

Sound was quite good with our low expectations.

It's going to add a solid pound (500 grams) to your backpack.

If this was $300 (U.S.) device, I'd be tearing it down. But at an advertised price at time of this writing at just under $70 it's a steal.
At this price range buy two, one for the kiddos and one for the bathroom.
How about one in the garage and one at the easy chair?
Or just have one as a backup.

Using compressed air I don't have to risk come into physical contact with the sensitive circuits involved and thus don't risk damaging them. The duster works exactly as stated and charges up quickly. title: Uninpressive...even on sale
text:
Let me start this by remarking that while I’ve been using Bluetooth earbuds since they came out, I only really have one set that is comparable to the linkbuds S, which is the Sennheiser CX plus buds I got a year ago. It’s a pretty even comparison from price and features (I got them both on sale).

If you just care about good sound for music, call clarity, and comfort, then you might just love the Linkbuds S. If you care about features like transparent hearing mode, battery life, noise canceling, or app usability…I’d recommend that you keep looking.

Sound: Even after taking pictures of my ears (awkward), testing tips for optimal ear pressure, and all the other things Sony wanted me to do, my CX plus buds out of the box sound better. 360 sound and app optimization was snake oil if you ask me. It is not a huge difference with most music, but I can really tell when listening to podcasts or audiobooks. The CX plus sound like the person is reading to you in a silent room, while the linkbuds sound no different than my 4 year old $30 generic buds. I even tried changing to the comply foam tips I use in all my buds, and while it usually improves things, I couldn’t tell the difference when using the linkbuds.

Call Clarity/Singal: A tie here. Both have very clear call clarity on both ends. I had no problems with singals dropping in Bluetooth heavy areas, both had similar range, and I carry my phone in my front pocket and never had drops with either.

Comfort/size: The Linkbuds S win this category by a massive margin. They are comfortable and conforming. So much so that this is the only aspect that gave me pause when returning them. This is where the foam tips usually come into play, but the linkbuds were just always comfortable regardless of the tips. MY CX plus buds get very uncomfortable after a couple hours which made me really appreciate the linkbuds in this regard.

ANC/Transparency mode: A big nope on both. For Transparency mode, my CX plus buds might have me spoiled, but I love that mode because it sounds natural, but boosted. The linkbuds makes everything sound tinny, like I’m walking around with a really cheap mic in my hands. I don’t really use ANC, but using foam tips seemed to do more than the ANC on the linkbuds, and even with them I could still hear everything around me. In comparison, I don’t use the CX plus ANC because it works so well that I get paranoid about something possibly sneaking up on me.

Battery life: Linkbuds S have a laughable battery life. With all the bells and whistles on I got about 2.25 hours, or 4 hours with everything off; both with the volume halfway. CX plus usually give me 6 with ANC on and 8 without at the same volume.

APP/Features: Both the Linkbuds S and CX plus have wonky apps. Some stuff with both are a little fiddly. I am sure that’s probably true with most apps the way software is rushed out anymore. Both have things I don’t like. Linkbuds S I can have Transparency/ANC or one feature and off, but not all 3 even through there are open commands (maybe I’m doing something wrong here). The CX plus allows me to do all three. Multipoint is done the same way, but credit goes to the linkbuds here because I can change to different devices without having to have both buds out. The Linkbuds have a feature that, if activated, can pause audio and turn transparency on when you speak…nice, but it also activates when you cough, hum, or clear your throat which I apparently do constantly, so I ended up not liking this feature at all and kept it off.

CXplus claim IPX7 to Linkbuds S’s IPX4. I’m not keen on testing either as I like my electronics dry.

Linkbuds S have a smaller, more pocket friendly case, CX Plus has a case with more battery. Linkbuds have a slightly rough matte texture, CX Plus is shiny smooth plastic. Both are subjective and will come down to personal preference.

I wish I had more buds to compare them to, but I’m cheap, so I don’t. Depending on what you’re after, these might be great for you (when on sale…a total rip at MSRP), but I returned them. Maybe the next generation will be better and I will be watching because they were pretty darn comfortable.

title: Brilliant.  It actually works.
text:
Plugable has always been my go-to brand for docking stations. They're the top producer in this product category for me - they pay attention to the details, and their products are actually tested in the weird corner cases that tend to trip up generic docks. I usually find them worth every penny of the price premium over other options because they actually work, and this dock is no exception.

I have been hunting for a dock for my ThinkPad P1 Gen 2 that supports three features: a 4K monitor at full resolution without DisplayLink, full 100W USB-C PD with no 16W deduction like many docks, and 2.5Gbps Ethernet. This one has all three features. And I'm pleased to report they all work exactly as they should.

Unlike another reviewer, I think this has exactly the right number of USB-A ports - I have keyboards, mice and other peripherals that all need a home, and this device has plenty of places to plug those in while still offering higher speed ports for more modern devices so they can coexist side by side.

I appreciate that a compliant Thunderbolt 4 cable is included, and it's actually pretty long, so you don't have to immediately run out and buy another cable. The power supply is also super beefy and from a major name brand, so it's legitimately high quality. Sometimes you actually get something for a price premium when you buy a top of the line product.

I was pleased to discover this dock lets me connect my Odyssey Ark 4K monitor to my ThinkPad at the full 165Hz refresh rate. I wouldn't necessarily depend on this and don't want to promise refresh rates higher than advertised, but in my case it worked - actually, better than plugging an HDMI cable directly into the computer, if you can believe that. This is a pretty challenging scenario and the dock handled it brilliantly.

Plugable is a great vendor and this is a top-of-the line docking station option. If you are setting up a flexible workstation and need the ability to quickly connect/disconnect a modern laptop, this is a top choice.

title: Fast name-brand SSD that works great at an unbelievable price
text:
Solidigm, a brand I hadn't previously heard of, is a company that has been newly formed as a subsidiary of South Korea's SK Hynix; it's been formed from the remnants of Intel's old SSD business. Both companies are well known for making quality products, and this one is no exception: the product is packaged well and comes with appropriate regulatory certifications.

More importantly, it offers a huge amount of storage - 2TB - at a crazy good price. Performance is rated at a very high level, too; I wasn't able to test that because I was using this drive in an external enclosure that limited its potential, but I certainly maxed out that case's speed. Other reviewers have posted CrystalDiskMark numbers that confirm this is a zippy performer!

There are a lot of mystery brands of SSDs out there, and it gives me quite a bit of confidence to buy a product directly from a chipmaker. At prices like this, it's even more of a no-brainer to pick this one. I'm tempted to upgrade all my devices with smaller SSDs to 2TB at this price. Highly recommended.

title: Far too underpowered for anything except very light usage
text:
This is an 8-port USB hub with three different kinds of ports: a few 5Mbps USB 3.0 ports, a few low speed USB 2.0 ports and a single charge only port. As this is limited to 5Mbps, you probably won't want to use it for newer USB 3.2 hard disks or other super-high-speed devices; this is best as a desktop accessory for connecting webcams, keyboards, mice, and other everyday gizmos.

What it's not very good at is charging. The entire 8 ports share a single 5V/2A wall adapter. This is woefully inadequate, as it's less than even a single phone's moderate fast charging current draw. Each USB port is required to be able to provide 500mA, so this hub is woefully underpowered by design; only four of the eight ports could use the full power. The on/off buttons can help you manage this to a certain extent, but if your goal in adding a hub is to inject more power into your connectivity, it's likely this won't be very useful at all.

There's one pretty niche scenario where the on/off buttons might be helpful. If you need the ability to switch between a few USB devices for testing purposes, this will let you do that without plugging and unplugging the devices. I build electronics as a hobby, and I'm often unplugging and replugging devices after loading new firmware onto them; this way, I can do that by just pushing the button twice instead to cut and resupply their power.

It doesn't help that the plastics for this hub are really, really poor: they're cheap and feel like they'll snap at the slightest provocation. I'm not super picky about materials and finishes for an affordable external hub, but this one's exceptionally bad. The power adapter is much better made than the hub itself.

For most everyday folks, these power switches are a gimmick and you'd be better off with a USB hub that has enough power to supply all of the devices you've connected. For an 8 port hub, I'd be looking to have at a minimum 4A of power available to share, and for a hub with USB 3 connectivity I'd be looking to have USB 3.2 10Gbps support. This device has neither.

title: Comfortable with good sound quality, but needs a better mute solution
text:
Summary: I've fallen in love with my Jabra Evolve 75 over the last two years of virtual meetings, so when this headset was offered for review with a similar design and feature set, I jumped at the chance to see if there was a better option out there.

Unfortunately, Poly fundamentally missed what I think is the most important feature of a unified communications (UC) headset - the ability to easily mute and unmute yourself during a call. The microphone boom doesn’t have a position sensor, so you have to rely on a teensy tiny little hard-to-find red mute button - and then listen to an intrusive voice slowly saying Mute Off before you can start talking.

It's a shame, because otherwise this headset is pretty decent. The dock is nice, voice quality is good, and it's comfortable to wear for long periods of time. The noise cancelling isn't very effective and a few other quality of life features the Jabra offers are missing, but the other fundamentals are sound.

Hopefully Poly can improve the mute functionality in a future version of this headset, because otherwise they'd have a real contender on their hands. Until then, I find it hard to recommend.

Voice quality

Voice quality was quite good, as you'd expect from a top end UC headset, with background noise blocked out well - the noise cancellation features worked much better here. I'd say the audio quality is pretty equivalent between this headset and the Jabra Evolve 75; the tonal quality sounds a little different between the two headsets, but I think it's just a Pepsi and Coke thing and I quickly adjusted.

Like all good UC headsets, the Focus provides sidetone (feeding your own voice back into your ear to prevent you from shouting), and the amount is an adjustable setting in the companion app. If your loved ones hate when you're on conference calls because you speak at a much higher than normal volume, this feature will definitely help.

Mute

This is a huge dealbreaker for me with the Poly headset and the primary reason for my low star rating. With my Jabra Evolve 75, I've gotten used to flipping up the microphone boom as my mute. It's easy, effective, and I can be 100% sure I'm not going to embarrass myself on a video call; like push to talk, except I can use it from anywhere even if I'm away from my computer. It's an innovation that's made conference calls a lot easier to manage, because I'm not bound to my conferencing software or a keypad for controls.

This headset inexplicably doesn't have this feature. Instead, mute can only be controlled by removing the headset entirely (useless if you are continuing to listen to a call, and impossible to verify that the sensor actually muted you), or by pressing a minuscule 6mm flush red button located underneath the mic boom at the base of the headset. The button is hard to find quickly and even harder to push because it is so low profile; it's bizarre that even the ANC controls are easier to find and operate than mute.

Obnoxiously, when you mute or unmute, a long and intrusive voice alert announces the mute status. This means that if you press the button to start talking, you're going to need to wait 3-5 seconds before you can start actually contributing to the call. The Jabra just says "Muted" or "Unmuted", which is much quicker, and it happens in under a second while you're still rotating the boom so it's less obtrusive; this Poly headset is more like "<beep> <pause> Mute <pause> Off". It sounds like a small thing, but it's maddening in practice.

There's theoretically a setting to disable the Mute Off announcement, but it doesn't work - even with that setting confirmed turned off and even after restarting the headset and verifying my firmware is up to date, I get the announcement anyway. Doubly frustrating.

Speaking of the mic boom, the Poly's doesn't snap into place when it's raised up - there's a slight detent but it doesn't secure there, so when you do flip it up you need to pay a bit more attention to getting it docked in the vertical position. The rotation also is stickier - rotating it up or down takes more force than on the Jabra - and the boom is much shorter than on the Jabra so it's harder to find and grasp while the headset is on your head.

Dock

The docks are very similar between the Jabra and the Poly, but I think I give the point to this Poly for the five-pogo-pin connector this headset uses instead of the Micro USB connector the Jabra uses, as it's just a little bit easier to align and dock. Having a place for your headset to charge is a wonderful feature and helps prevent the headset from getting lost. (If you do forget to charge it, the headset will allow you to plug in and charge while using it, too.)

Call Feedback

I don't like the call feedback lights on the Poly: it indicates you're in call with an animation of two tiny blinking blue pinpoint lights. The Evolve 75 has a large glowing red ring, which makes it very clear to guests and visitors that you're in the middle of a call. I miss that feature here.

Noise Cancelling

The Poly's noise cancelling for the headphones is, frankly, not very good. With it on or off, I still can hear the air purifier in my workspace at a very high level - notably worse than the Jabra Evolve 75. While I could notice a small reduction in certain frequency ranges with it on, there's still a ton of background noise and I can even hear distant road noise. I would say this is the least effective ANC of any headset I own.

If ANC is important to you, you should consider a different headset. (To be fair, this is not the top of the line product Poly offers and perhaps the Focus 2 is better as they identify ANC as one of the upgrades, but on this headset, it's so ineffective I barely consider it to have the feature at all.)

Music Quality

This is actually pretty close between the two headsets and both are good, although I think the Jabra edges out slightly with more balanced sound on the low end. The Poly's sound tends toward booming bass, so if you enjoy more oomph in your music, you may prefer it; I find it a little overpowering and think the Jabra's sound is more accurate and true to the original source. Neither headset is audiophile grade and my Sony XM series headphones are dramatically better than both, but it's good enough that you won't feel the need to swap just to listen to some music between conference calls. I'd say that the performance is about equivalent to a $99 dedicated pair of headphones.

Open Mic

This is a feature which allows you to listen to your environment. Because the ANC is so poor, I didn't really find this necessary and prefer to just remove my headset to feel 'present' when speaking to guests in real life, but it is a nice addition that my Evolve 75 doesn't have. (The new Evolve2 75, which I have not tried, does add a similar feature.)

Interface

Setting aside the elephant in the room of the terrible mute controls, I otherwise like the controls on this a little more than the Jabra Evolve 75. The volume knob is a rotating knob, and you get an ascending/descending tone as you make adjustments. The power switch and ANC are both slide toggles and are in reasonable locations, and there are easy to find play/skip forward/skip back buttons.

The Poly has a sensor that detects whether the headset is on your head and pauses your music when you remove it (in addition to other features, like muting calls). I'm not sure I love this - the sensor got it wrong a few times in my testing and I was confused why I couldn't hear my music until I removed it and replaced it on my head. But when it works, it is a nice feature so I don't end up blasting thumping music from the dock after removing the headset to talk with someone.

Comfort

Both headsets are quite comfortable to wear, and I find myself forgetting I'm wearing either after just a few minutes. The Jabra relies on a single integrated padded headband, while this one has a dual metal-band-and-inner-padding system. I honestly can't tell the difference while they're on my head. The structure seems a little lighter weight on this headset, so long term longevity will be something to watch, but for now they seem well built.

Dual Pairing

Like the Jabra Evolve 75, this headset supports dual device pairing, so you can be paired to your phone and laptop simultaneously, and you can switch between the two depending on scenario seamlessly. The switching works great and you can be listening to music, then hop into a conference call the next minute without any reconfiguration.

App

The iPhone companion app, PLT Hub, looks super dated; the screens aren't designed for newer iPhones, so you'll see huge bars at the top and bottom while using it. It seems to more or less work, but a bit of updating to bring it up to modern UI standards would be appreciated.

Case and Portability

The ear cups rotate 90 degrees so the headset can sit flatter for transport, which is a nice touch. There is a case included, but it's a thin bag rather than a rigid form, so the headset isn't very well protected when inside - you'l definitely want to baby this more than the clamshell case that the Evolve 75 ships with. It's thinner and lighter, though, so tradeoffs...

Interestingly, while the rest of the headset has Poly branding, the case still is branded Plantronics as if it's leftover inventory from a previous model.

Conclusion

This is a fairly nice mid-range headset that doesn't fit into my workflow because of the poor mute design. Pretty much anything would have been better - the mic boom should control mute, for sure, but even letting me reconfigure the call button on the right earcup as mute would have made all the difference in the world. I'm not sure what Poly was thinking, missing out on the most important aspect of a UC headset while getting most other details right, and I hope they can address this glaring omission in a future version of the product.

title: Stay put during exercise, great sound quality, great battery life, physical buttons
text:
I am testing these out for my Mom. It will be her first bluetooth headphones ever. she is almost 70 so I need them to be easy. I have owned 6+ paris of BT headphones, so I tend to know what is good and what is not.

Pros:
- Quick bluetooth sync
- Pretty pink color
- Good battery life; the case battery lasts forever... forever.... forever (sandlot anyone?)
- Good sound, I think these have plenty of bass/mids for earbuds, not sure why people are complaining
- Volume has plenty of range (loud enough for 70 year old on phone calls)
- Phone calls sound great on both ends of the call
- they stay in your ear no matter what
- Physical buttons for pause/volume (vs. the tap to pause).
- Comfortable, It took me about 5 hours straight to feel any sort of discomfort from wearing these and even then it wasn't bad.

Cons:
The ear wrap gets annoying after a while, but they will always stay in your ear! Great for exercising.

Summary, I think these will be fantastic for my mom. She will mostly use them for calls, but occasionally for music. I am personally a huge fan of the physical buttons for answer/end call, pause, volume, etc. The only think you have to get used to is if you answer a call with your phone and then try to put the headphone in, the end call button is easy to press on accident. After hanging up on a few people you get used to it pretty quick and figure out how to put the device in your ear without hanging up on someone.

I hope this helps!

title: Great 4K monitor for multiple uses
text:
This is a great 4K monitor, especially for gaming. I am running it as my main Gaming monitor connected to a RTX 3080 Ti, and its great for playing most games at 165hz on high graphics settings. Adaptive Sync works great, and I haven't had any problem with tearing or anything. The picture quality is very good, and HDR works well too. This is my first time using a curved screen as my primary monitor, and its definitely very noticeable, but I haven't found it too distracting. If you stare at it you will notice it, but after a few hours my eyes seem to have adjusted to it and I don't even notice it most of the time anymore.

One of the cool features included with this monitor is an Ultrawide mode (Menu > Game > Ultrawide Game View), where instead of running in 4K (3840 × 2160) you can switch to Ultrawide resolution (3440 x 1440). There are some caveats though, and I think make it less useful. First, you can't enable the mode without disabling Adaptive Sync. When Ultrawide mode is enabled, you'll see black bars (think "letterbox") on the top and bottom of the screen. The monitor will no longer report 4K (2160p) as a supported resolution, and will report that (3440 x 1440) is the native resolution. In Windows, it also acted like a new/different monitor and threw off my multi-monitor setup when toggling the Ultrawide mode. Out of the games I play, the only one that really supported Ultrawide is Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, but ultimately it just wasn't worth the tradeoff for me so I don't use it.

The LED lighting (Menu Game > Infinity Core Lighting) on the front/back is pretty cool, but as a computer monitor on a desk the front lights are not very visible because they are so recessed. The back light does create a cool effect though, especially in darker lighting. You have the option to turn it off, enable just the back lighting, or both front and back. There are a handful of lighting effects available, or you can choose a static color. There is also a "CoreSync" option which adjusts the brightness based on what is on the screen, but is only compatible with a single color. Personally I like the "Rainbow" mode the best, which rotates through colors.

The stand has a fairly large footprint, but this is a pretty big monitor, so that makes sense. The monitor does include a metal plate for mounting it, but be aware that the monitor is pretty heavy, so make sure your stand can handle it, or if mounting to a wall that its secured well.

Overall I think this is a great monitor for gaming, movies, and productivity. I love how much real estate there is for working multiple applications. With a 100% scale you can really use 4 apps at once (one in each quarter) effectively. Lots of applications do look a little funny when maximized though, and most websites will just leave with you lots of dead space because they aren't designed to be used on such a high resolution. I just use that as an excuse to never really go over half my screen for an application, which just gives me more room for multitasking. I'm really loving this monitor, and feel like its one of the best out there for mixed use (gaming, media, productivity/work).

title: Great for organizing LOTS of batteries
text:
This case is amazing. I went from using 4 different containers of different sizes to this one, which takes almost the same amount of space in my drawer because this one is laid out so well. Also, I felt like I had a lot of batteries before, but I probably didn't even fill half of it. Guess I need more!

title: Light weight and works great
text: I got this for my father who is a security guard in a bad part of town. He wears it on his uniform on his patrols. It is a great size and isn't to heavy to wear. The battery life is good. He wears it on an 8 hours shift and it makes it through the shift on a charge. The video quality and sound quality are good. This camera really makes me feel at ease. title: Worked great until the warranty expired!
text: I have this tv mounted on the wall above my treadmill. It had a nice clear picture and I was very pleased with it. I use it for maybe 5 hours a week so it doesn't get a lot of use. Last week I noticed hundreds of very thin faint black horizontal lines over the screen from top to bottom. Maybe if I wasn't so close to the screen I wouldn't notice them but now that I see them I can't not see them and it spoils my enjoyment. I checked to see when I bought it to see if I could get a replacement but the warranty expired last month. Oh well it's still usable so I'll keep it until it dies.

title: Huge LED heatsink, could run all day at 100%! Pro quality gear!
text:
This is built very well. I couldn't be happier with this overall.
Quiet fan silently blows heat out with the light, ultra bright LED, aluminum light diffuser creates zero hot spots or halos, just perfect light. 10-100% light settings, in 1% increments. The heat sink has a ton of surface area and is over an inch thick, it's hard to capture in a picture just how nice that heatsink is, it keeps the LED very happy, so it will have a long life. I have no way to test lumen output, but this definitely looks to be rated correctly on lumen and color temp. Very high CRI rating.
AC adapter works great, barely gets warm after 15 mins on max brightness. The light is limited to 60w on batteries, which is still so bright it's not much of a loss.
The support bar is aluminum with many position detents, it won't be moving. The handle is plastic and can be put into the support bar in 3 positions and locks in firmly.
The display is very easy to see, shows light setting and LED temp in C. The tactile wheel feels good and is easy to use, and is a button when pressed. It got up to 40C and there was no noticable change in the fan speed. In the special modes the fan does not run, I speculate this is because the LED is not running continuously, as it is being flashed or dimmed and not making much heat. Special modes are paparazzi, firework, bad bulbs, thunder flash, TV, and SOS. The first 5 have 9 settings for frequency, and all can have light intensity changed as normal.
Hopefully I've covered anything you were curious about! :-)

I will UPDATE this review if anything changes, good or bad! I take Vine seriously and am always honest in my reviews. Thank you for reading! If you have any questions please submit them using the 'Customer questions & answers' section just above the reviews area.

title: Lights and buttons
text: I like the sound quite well. What I don't care for is how difficult it is to see the screen. Day or night. At night the back light is overwhelming...too blue, making it difficult to see anything. Buttons are difficult to press and work. Cost is too high for such a lower value item.
